summary: Describes how to use the Stac LZS data compression algorithm to compress PPP packets using a DCP header. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1967 defines how to use Stac LZS compression with PPP. Its packet header can report whether data is compressed, detect some packet errors and request that compression histories be reset.

questions: how to compress ppp with stac lzs
what is the dcp header in ppp
how does ppp stac lzs resynchronize
what is a reset request in ppp compression
subtitle: How PPP carries Stac LZS compressed data with reset and error-detection signals.

tldr.problem: Compression that uses shared history can lose synchronization when packets are dropped, damaged or arrive out of order.
tldr.mechanism: LZS-DCP carries compressed or uncompressed data with a DCP header that signals resets, and can add sequence numbers and a check byte.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC describes an enhanced PPP use of Stac LZS and says the pending TIA/EIA-655 standard uses the protocol.

today: RFC 1967 is an Informational memo published in August 1996, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC says the pending TIA/EIA-655 standard uses LZS-DCP.

sections.title: Purpose of LZS-DCP
sections.content:
PPP can carry multiple network protocols over point-to-point links, and its Compression Control Protocol negotiates compression. RFC 1967 describes using the Stac LZS compression algorithm with a Data Compression Protocol (DCP) header inside PPP.

The memo presents LZS-DCP as an enhanced version of the earlier PPP Stac LZS protocol. Its changes include signaling resets in each packet, indicating whether data is compressed, and allowing sequence numbers and a Longitudinal Check Byte to be used together.
sections.plainLanguage: LZS-DCP carries Stac LZS-compressed data over a PPP link. Its header adds signals that help the two ends detect and recover from problems with shared compression history.

sections.title: Carrying Data over PPP
sections.content:
Before sending LZS-DCP packets, PPP must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and the Compression Control Protocol must be Opened. One LZS-DCP datagram is carried in the PPP Information field. The PPP Protocol value is 00FD for a compressed datagram or 00FB when compression is negotiated separately on individual links to the same destination.

The compressed input starts with the PPP Protocol ID followed by the original Information field. Link Control Protocol and Network Control Protocol packets must not be carried inside LZS-DCP packets. PPP padding is not allowed, although zero octets may follow compressed data as LZS padding.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP carries one LZS-DCP datagram in its Information field after the compression protocol has been negotiated. The packet's PPP Protocol value identifies which LZS-DCP mode applies.

sections.title: The DCP Header and Checks
sections.content:
The packet includes the PPP Protocol field, a DCP header and data, with history number, sequence number and Longitudinal Check Byte (LCB) fields when negotiated. The one-octet DCP header indicates compressed or uncompressed data and contains Reset-Ack and Reset-Request bits. Its reserved bits must be zero, and its Control/Data bit must be zero for this PPP use.

A sequence number can identify dropped or misordered packets. The LCB is calculated from the uncompressed datagram and can detect data errors. A history number identifies which compression history applies when multiple histories are negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: The DCP header marks compressed data and carries reset signals. Optional sequence and check fields help the receiver detect missing, reordered or damaged data.

sections.title: Recovering Compression History
sections.content:
When compression history is used, the compressor and decompressor must keep matching histories. A dropped, damaged or misordered datagram can make them differ, and the decompressor cannot continue correctly with an out-of-sync history. The sequence number and LCB can identify receive failures according to the negotiated check mode.

After a receive failure, the receiver sends a Reset-Request for the affected history and discards later data for that history until it receives a Reset-Ack. The transmitter clears that history and sends a packet with the acknowledgment bit set. When the history count is zero, the history is cleared at the start of every datagram, so the protocol does not depend on reliable, in-order delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: If the two ends no longer have matching compression histories, the receiver requests a reset for that history. It discards later data for that history until the sender acknowledges the reset.

sections.title: Negotiating LZS-DCP Settings
sections.content:
The LZS-DCP Configuration Option is used with the Compression Control Protocol to agree on compression settings. It has Type 23, Length 6, a two-octet History Count, a Check Mode and a Process Mode. If the peers do not agree, no compression is used.

A History Count of one is the default and maintains one history; zero means the history is cleared at the beginning of every packet. Check Mode selects no check, LCB, sequence number, or both; the default is sequence number plus LCB. Process Mode determines whether uncompressed packets update the compression history.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers agree on how many histories to keep and which checks to use. If they cannot agree on the settings, they send data without this compression.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: Extension bit; set to 1 for the one-octet header.

fields.name: R-R
fields.desc: Requests a reset for this history.

fields.name: C/D
fields.desc: Control/Data bit; zero for PPP data packets.
